# Math

Numerics: signal processing in both domains, estimation and fitting, interpolation, statistics, randomness and units. Everything here is plain `Double`/`Float` Kotlin with no GPU and no window, so it runs in a box, a test or a headless docs capture equally well.

18 source file(s), 1575 public symbol(s), 1190 of them carrying KDoc. Everything below is the documentation that lives beside the code — the same text the [completion documentation panel](../completion_doc_browser.md) shows in the editor. ## Functions.kt { #functions-kt }

The `Fn` toolkit: one-dimensional signals as values you can build, compose, sample and draw.

Nearly everything lives inside the [`Functions`](math.md#functions-kt-functions) object, and most of it as extension functions,
so callers normally work inside `with(Functions) { ... }`. A `Functions.Fn` is an evaluator
plus the `Functions.Domain` it is meant to be sampled over (default `0.0..1.0`). Sources —
`sin`, `saw`, `triangle`, `square`, the `pulseTrain` / `pulseBurst` family, the noise and
`fbm` generators, and keyframe interpolants such as `catmullRomSpline` and `monotoneCubic` —
combine through arithmetic operators, through chainable `Fn` extensions (`stretch`, `repeat`,
`fold`, `quantize`, `echo`, `convolve`, `blur`, ...), and through reusable `FnTransform`
pipelines applied with `/`. Arrangement in time is `timeline { }` and the `List<Fn>`
combinators (`sequence`, `randomPermute`, `morph`, `stack`, `average`).

Every combinator also records an `FnGraphNode` recipe alongside the closure (see
`FunctionGraph.kt`), which is what makes graphs inspectable and rewritable rather than opaque
lambdas. On the output side: `toDoubleArray` and the `sample*` helpers for numbers, `toFLine`
for drawing, `plotHtml` for a self-contained plot, and `Fn.plot`, which displays into the
active `Box` and throws when there is none (`Box.plot` takes the `Fn` explicitly instead).

[`RbfKernel`](math.md#functions-kt-rbfkernel), [`RbfKernels`](math.md#functions-kt-rbfkernels) and [`RbfInterpolator`](math.md#functions-kt-rbfinterpolator) at the top of the file are the scattered-data
fitter behind `Functions.rbf`; it solves a dense n×n system per construction, so it is sized
for handfuls of control points, not thousands.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/Functions.kt`

**Used in:** [Functions to FLine examples (Field graphics)](../functions_examples.md)

### RbfKernel { #functions-kt-rbfkernel }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">RbfKernel</span></code>

A radial basis function: how strongly a control point still counts at distance `r` from the x being evaluated.

### RbfKernels { #functions-kt-rbfkernels }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">RbfKernels</span></code>

The ready-made [`RbfKernel`](math.md#functions-kt-rbfkernel) family behind `Functions.rbf`: four parameter-free kernels as values, and four shape-parameter kernels as factories.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">linear</span></code> | `r` itself: interpolation degenerates to straight segments between neighbouring points. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">quadratic</span></code> | `r²`. Grows quickly with distance, so distant control points pull hard on the fit. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">cubic</span></code> | `r³`. The stiffest of the polynomial kernels; smooth, but prone to overshoot far from data. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">thinPlate</span></code> | The thin-plate spline kernel `r²·ln r`, with the removable singularity at `r = 0` defined as zero. The default for `Functions.rbf`, and the one to reach for first: it needs no shape parameter, so it cannot be mis-scaled. Note that it is *negative* for `r < 1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">gaussian</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">epsilon</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | A Gaussian bump `exp(-(εr)²)` — the one genuinely local kernel here, so influence dies away within roughly `1/ε` of each control point. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">multiquadric</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">c</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | `sqrt(r² + c²)` — a softened `linear`, rounded off near `r = 0` over a width of about `c`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">inverseMultiquadric</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">c</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | `1 / sqrt(r² + c²)` — decays with distance, so the fit stays local-ish; `c` sets the width. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">inverseQuadratic</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">c</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | `1 / (r² + c²)` — the fastest-decaying of the inverse kernels; `c` sets the width. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Fn</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">sampleUniform</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">count</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">sampleDomain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ClosedRange</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="o">&#42;</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">includeEnd</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Sample</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | `count` evenly-spaced observations across the given range, as `Sample`s. `includeEnd` decides whether the last one lands on the upper bound. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Fn</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">sampleJittered</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">count</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">sampleDomain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ClosedRange</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="o">&#42;</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">jitter</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.25</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Sample</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | `count` stratified observations across the given range, one per cell, displaced by up to half `jitter` of a cell width. Deterministic in `seed`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Fn</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">sampleRandom</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">count</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">sampleDomain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Domain</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">domain</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Sample</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | `count` observations at pseudo-random positions across `sampleDomain` — unstratified, so expect clumps and gaps; `sampleJittered` is usually the better-behaved choice. |

Deterministic in `seed`. |

## LeastSquares.kt { #leastsquares-kt }

A Levenberg–Marquardt nonlinear least-squares solver, pure Kotlin and self-contained.

`leastSquares` takes an initial parameter vector and a `residuals: (DoubleArray) -> DoubleArray`
lambda and minimises half the squared residual norm. [`LeastSquaresOptions`](math.md#leastsquares-kt-leastsquaresoptions) controls the
iteration cap, the damping schedule and three convergence tolerances; [`LeastSquaresResult`](math.md#leastsquares-kt-leastsquaresresult)
reports the parameters, final residuals, cost, iteration count, an `rms`, and a `reason` string
— one of "gradient", "step", "improvement", "no accepted step" or "max iterations".

The Jacobian is central finite differences **by default**, so you never have to supply
derivatives, but each iteration then costs `2 * parameters` extra residual evaluations. Pass an
explicit `jacobian` — or, easier, write the residuals in [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) arithmetic and call
`leastSquaresAD`, which derives an exact Jacobian by reverse-mode automatic differentiation — to
trade those `2n` evaluations for one backward sweep and get derivatives that are exact rather
than truncated. Omitting `jacobian` leaves the historic path bit-for-bit unchanged.

The damped normal equations are solved by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting; a singular
system or a non-finite candidate raises the damping and retries (up to 12 times per iteration)
rather than failing. Non-finite initial residuals throw.

## autodiff.kt { #autodiff-kt }

Reverse-mode automatic differentiation over `Double` scalars — exact gradients for ordinary
Kotlin arithmetic, in one pass, whatever the expression's size.

Every gradient in Field before this file was a *numerical* one: `fitGradient` central-differences
its loss (`FunctionFit.kt`), `leastSquares` central-differences its Jacobian. That costs
`2·n` extra evaluations per step and buys a truncation/round-off compromise you have to tune with
an `fdStep`. Reverse mode costs one forward pass plus one backward sweep for *all* `n`
derivatives, and the answer is exact to the last few ulps.

### The shape of it

[`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) is a scalar that remembers how it was made. Arithmetic on [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) values appends to an [`ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape)
— a flat array of (value, up-to-two parents, up-to-two local partials) — so
`(a * b + sin(c)) / 2.0` reads exactly like `Double` arithmetic and quietly records a graph. The
backward sweep walks that array once in reverse accumulating adjoints. Because every node has at
most two parents, the tape is three arrays of primitives and no object churn beyond the [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad)
handles themselves.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val g = grad { p -> (p[0] - 3.0).sq() + 2.0 * (p[1] + 1.0).sq() }
g(doubleArrayOf(0.0, 0.0))          // [-6.0, 4.0], exact

val (v, d) = valueAndDerivative(0.4) { x -> exp(-x * x) * sin(6.0 * x) }
```

`grad` returns a *function*, so it composes with the optimizers in `autodiff_optimize.kt`
(`minimize`, `adam`, `sgd`, `lbfgs`) without a wrapper. `gradAt`, `valueAndGrad`, `jacobian` and
`hessian` are the immediate forms.

### Forward mode

[`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2) is a second-order forward-mode number (value, first derivative, second derivative along a
direction). It is the right tool when there is one input and many outputs — the reverse of
reverse mode — and it is what makes `hessian` *exact* rather than a finite difference of an exact
gradient: `vᵀHv` falls out of a single [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2) pass, and polarisation recovers the off-diagonal
entries. See `directionalDerivative` and `secondDerivative`.

### The kink convention

`abs`, `min`, `max` and `relu` are not differentiable at their kink, so a convention has to be
chosen. This library **splits the derivative evenly at an exact tie**: `min(a, b)` with `a == b`
sends 0.5 to each argument, and `relu` (which is `max(x, 0)`) has derivative 0.5 at zero. That is
not an arbitrary pick — it is precisely what a central difference reports at a kink, so the
analytic gradient and the finite-difference oracle *agree there too*, and `abs(x) = max(x, -x)`
comes out with derivative 0 at zero, which is the minimum-norm subgradient. (PyTorch instead
defines `relu'(0) = 0`; the choice here is the internally consistent one.)

### What is not covered

- **Mutation.** [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) is immutable; there is no in-place `+=` on a tracked value beyond rebinding
  a `var`, which is fine and does the right thing.
- **Control flow** is differentiated *as taken*: an `if (x > 0.0)` records only the branch that
  ran, which is the correct derivative of the piecewise function everywhere except at the
  switch-over. Comparisons on [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) therefore return plain `Boolean` and carry no derivative.
- **Piecewise-constant ops** (`floor`, `round`, `sign`, `quantize`) have derivative 0 by
  definition, and no finite-difference oracle exists at their jumps.
- **Third and higher derivatives** are not available. `hessian` is exact; a third-order term
  would need a `Dual3` or a nestable tape and neither is here.
- **Tape size** grows with the number of *operations executed*, not with `n`. A loss over 100k
  samples builds a 100k-node tape per evaluation; that is the memory cost of reverse mode and it
  is not chunked or checkpointed.

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">dot</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AD</span></code> | The dot product of two equal-length lists of tracked values. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">sumOfSquares</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AD</span></code> | The sum of squares — the squared Euclidean norm. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">norm</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AD</span></code> | The Euclidean norm `√Σxᵢ²`. Its derivative is undefined at the origin, where `√` reports ∞. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">maxOf</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AD</span></code> | The largest element, folded pairwise with `max` (so ties split evenly at each comparison). |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">logSumExp</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AD</span></code> | `ln Σ eˣⁱ`, shifted by the maximum so it never overflows — the smooth maximum, and the numerically safe way to write a soft-min/soft-max penalty inside a differentiated loss. |

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">ADTape</span></code>

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">variables</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | `variable` for a whole vector, in order — the usual way to start a gradient. |

## autodiff_forward.kt { #autodiff-forward-kt }

Forward-mode automatic differentiation to **second order** — the other half of `autodiff.kt`.

A [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2) is a truncated Taylor series `(v, v', v'')` carried along a single direction. Every
operation propagates all three components, so one evaluation of an expression in [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2)
arithmetic returns the value, the directional first derivative and the directional *curvature* at
once — no tape, no backward sweep, no allocation beyond three boxed doubles per node.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val t = taylor2(0.6) { x -> exp(-x * x) * sin(6.0 * x) }
t.value; t.first; t.second      // f, f', f'' at 0.6, all exact
```

### When to reach for this rather than the tape

Reverse mode (`grad`) wins when there are many inputs and one output — a loss over a parameter
vector. Forward mode wins in the opposite shape (one input, many outputs: a parametric curve and
every quantity derived from it) and, crucially, it is the only one of the two here that reaches
second order. `hessian` in `autodiff.kt` is built on this file: `vᵀHv` is exactly `Dual2.second`
after a pass seeded along `v`.

The op vocabulary deliberately mirrors `autodiff.kt` name for name — `sin`, `exp`, `tanh`, `max`,
`pow` and friends are overloaded on both [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) and [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2), so the *same* expression body can be
written once against a shape and evaluated either way (see [`ADFunction2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-adfunction2)).

### Conventions and gaps

- The kink convention matches `autodiff.kt`: `max` / `min` split evenly at an exact tie, so
  `relu''` is 0 everywhere and `relu'(0)` is 0.5.
- `pow` with a *tracked* exponent is evaluated as `exp(b · ln a)` and therefore requires a
  strictly positive base; the constant-exponent `Dual2.pow` has no such restriction.
- Third and higher derivatives are not represented. A `Dual3` would be a mechanical extension of
  the same chain rule; it is not here.

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">ln</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Natural logarithm. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">sqrt</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Square root. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">cbrt</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Cube root. Written out rather than delegated to `Dual2.pow`, because `Math.pow` is undefined for a negative base at a fractional exponent while the cube root is perfectly well defined there. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">sin</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Sine of an angle in radians. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">cos</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Cosine of an angle in radians. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">tan</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Tangent. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">atan</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Arc tangent. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">cosh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Hyperbolic cosine. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">tanh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Hyperbolic tangent. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">abs</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Absolute value; the derivative is 0 at exactly zero, and the curvature is 0 everywhere. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">relu</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The rectifier `max(x, 0)`; derivative 0.5 at exactly zero, curvature 0 everywhere. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">sigmoid</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The logistic sigmoid `1/(1+e⁻ˣ)`; `σ'' = σ(1-σ)(1-2σ)`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">softplus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The smooth rectifier `ln(1+eˣ)`; its derivative is the sigmoid and its curvature `σ(1-σ)`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">floor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Floor — piecewise constant, so both derivatives are 0. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">ceil</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Ceiling — piecewise constant, so both derivatives are 0. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">round</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Nearest integer — piecewise constant, so both derivatives are 0. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">pow</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">base</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">exponent</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | `a` raised to the power `b`, both tracked, as `exp(b · ln a)`; needs a strictly positive base. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">max</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The larger of two, selecting a branch; an exact tie averages both, matching the AD convention. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">max</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The larger of a tracked value and a constant. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">min</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The smaller of two, selecting a branch; an exact tie averages both. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">min</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The smaller of a tracked value and a constant. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">hypot</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | `√(x²+y²)`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">atan2</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Two-argument arc tangent, correct in all four quadrants. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">sumDual</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The sum of a list. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">meanDual</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The arithmetic mean of a list. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">sumOfSquaresDual</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The sum of squares of a list. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">dotDual</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The dot product of two equal-length lists. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">normDual</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The Euclidean norm of a list. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">taylor2</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">f</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The value, first and second derivative of a single-variable function at `x`, in one pass. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">gradForward</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">f</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ADFunction2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span></code> | The gradient by forward mode — `n` passes, one per axis. |

### Dual2 { #autodiff-forward-kt-dual2 }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Dual2</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">first</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">second</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

A second-order forward-mode number: a value together with its first and second derivative along one direction.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The plain value `f`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">first</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The first derivative `df/dt` along the seeded direction. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">second</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The second derivative `d²f/dt²` along the seeded direction. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">plus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Sum, componentwise. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">plus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Sum with a constant, which shifts only the value. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">minus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Difference, componentwise. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">minus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Difference with a constant. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">times</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Product; the second order picks up the `2·u'·w'` cross term. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">times</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Product with a constant, which scales all three orders. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">div</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Quotient, as `this * other.reciprocal()`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">div</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Quotient by a constant. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">unaryMinus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Negation. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">operator</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">unaryPlus</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Identity. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">chain</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">fv</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">d1</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">d2</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Applies an outer scalar function given its value and its first two derivatives at `value` — the second-order chain rule `(f∘u)'' = f''·u'² + f'·u''`, and the single place every unary op in this file is implemented. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">reciprocal</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Reciprocal `1/x`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">sq</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | The square `x²`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">pow</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">exponent</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | `x` raised to a constant power, valid for negative `value` at integer exponents. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">pow</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">exponent</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | `x` raised to a constant integer power. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">clamp</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">lo</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">hi</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code> | Clamps into `[lo, hi]`, with the even-split tie convention on each boundary. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> |  |

### ADFunction2 { #autodiff-forward-kt-adfunction2 }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">typealias</span> <span class="nc">ADFunction2</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code>

A scalar function of a vector written once against [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2), so it can be handed to both `hessian` and `directionalDerivative` without being restated.

## autodiff_geometry.kt { #autodiff-geometry-kt }

Differentiable geometry: tracked vectors, planar inverse kinematics on an `FLine` chain, and a
differentiable circle packing — the "things that produce pixels" end of the AD layer.

[`ADVec2`](math.md#autodiff-geometry-kt-advec2) and [`ADVec3`](math.md#autodiff-geometry-kt-advec3) are pairs and triples of [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad), not a parallel numeric tower: they convert to
and from Field's own [`Vec2`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec2) / `Vec3` (which are the generated, *mutable*, float-backed
`Vector2f` / `Vector3f`), and everything they do is expressed in the same scalar ops as the rest of
`autodiff.kt`. They exist because writing `(joint - target).length()` reads better in a loss than
unrolling the components by hand, not because vectors need special derivative rules.

### Inverse kinematics

`solveIk` is the demonstration that earns the layer: a planar chain of fixed-length links whose
joint angles are found by minimising `|endEffector - target|²` with exact gradients. Forward
kinematics is a cumulative sum of angles and a running position — perfectly differentiable — so
L-BFGS reaches a sub-micron reach in tens of iterations, and the result is an `FLine` you can draw.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val chain = IkChain(vec(120f, 300f), doubleArrayOf(90.0, 80.0, 70.0, 55.0))
val solved = solveIk(chain, vec(360f, 150f))
showPlane(listOf(chain.toFLine(solved.angles)))
```

A pure reach objective is under-determined for more than two links, so `IkOptions.smoothness`
offers a curvature penalty between consecutive links. It is off by default and it is **not** free:
the two terms genuinely compete, so a positive smoothness buys an elegant pose at the price of a
little reach error, and near the base — where reaching at all needs tight folds — that price is
visible. Measured on the four-link chain below with `smoothness = 0.02`: a target 216 units out
still reaches to under a thousandth of a unit, but a target 5 units from the anchor settles 2.6
units short. `IkSolution.reachError` always reports the truth; nothing here pretends to have
converged when it has traded away accuracy.

### Packing

`packCircles` minimises pairwise overlap and wall penetration under a gentle pull toward the
centre. Every term is a `relu(...)²` hinge, which is exactly where the even-split kink convention
in `autodiff.kt` matters: at the moment two circles touch, the penalty's gradient is *half* what a
naive one-sided rule would give, and the packing settles rather than chattering.

## autodiff_optimize.kt { #autodiff-optimize-kt }

Gradient-descent optimizers that consume the exact gradients from `autodiff.kt` — `sgd`, `adam`
and `lbfgs`, behind one `minimize` front door.

All three are **deterministic given their seed** and all three record a full `OptimizeRun.losses` trajectory
which you can hand straight to `showSignals("loss" to run.losses)` and look at. That discipline is the
same one [`FnEvolveRun`](function.md#functionevolve-kt-fnevolverun) and [`FnFitRun`](function.md#functionfit-kt-fnfitrun) keep, and for the same reason: a fitted gesture in live art
is only usable if it comes back identical tomorrow.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val run = minimize(doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0), OptimizeOptions(method = OptimizeMethod.LBFGS)) { p ->
    (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq()   // Rosenbrock
}
run.x          // ~[1, 1]
run.losses     // the trajectory, ready to plot
```

### Which one

- `lbfgs` is the right default for a smooth deterministic objective with a handful to a few
  hundred parameters: it builds a curvature model from the last `m` steps and takes
  Newton-shaped strides, so it reaches machine-precision minima in tens of iterations where Adam
  is still crawling. It needs the objective to actually be smooth; a kinked or noisy loss will
  make its line search flail.
- `adam` is the robust workhorse for a rough, kinked or stochastic landscape, and the one that
  tolerates a badly scaled parameter vector without preconditioning.
- `sgd` with momentum is here because it is sometimes what you want *artistically* — a slower,
  visibly settling trajectory with a tunable inertia, which reads as motion rather than as a
  solver converging.

The line search inside `lbfgs` is backtracking Armijo, which guarantees monotone descent but not
the curvature (Wolfe) condition; the L-BFGS memory therefore skips any update pair with
non-positive curvature rather than letting an indefinite model through.

## correlations.kt { #correlations-kt }

Measures of statistical dependence between two equal-length `DoubleArray`s, batch and rolling.

[`StatsDependence`](math.md#correlations-kt-statsdependence) carries the batch versions: `pearson`, `spearman` (Pearson on average-tie
ranks), `kendallTauB`, `chatterjeeXi` (aliased as `xi`), `distanceCorrelation` and
`micTicNaive`. Kendall's tau-b and distance correlation are both O(n²) in time, and distance
correlation additionally materialises two n×n matrices, so neither suits long series.

[`RollingDistanceCorrelation`](math.md#correlations-kt-rollingdistancecorrelation) holds a fixed window and updates its maintained row and grand sums
in O(n) per `push`; [`RollingXiCorrelation`](math.md#correlations-kt-rollingxicorrelation) only keeps the window and recomputes xi from
scratch. All of it is pure Kotlin with no external dependency. Note the block comment below,
which is explicit that `micTicNaive` is an equipartition-grid approximation and not MICe/TICe —
do not expect matching values.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/correlations.kt`

**Used in:** [Values over time: interpolants & keyframes](../interpolants_examples.md), [Which of these signals actually depend on each other?](../statistics_examples.md)

### Top-level functions { #correlations-kt-functions }

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">main</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | A scratch demo rather than part of the API: prints every coefficient in this file for `y = x²` over an x grid symmetric about zero — the textbook case where `pearson` reads about 0 while the dependence is in fact total, so `StatsDependence.chatterjeeXi` and `StatsDependence.distanceCorrelation` read high. |

### StatsDependence { #correlations-kt-statsdependence }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">StatsDependence</span></code>

The batch dependence coefficients: hand any of these two equal-length `DoubleArray`s and get one number back per notion of "related" — `pearson` for linear association, `spearman` and `kendallTauB` for monotone association on ranks, `chatterjeeXi` for "is y a function of x", `distanceCorrelation` for dependence of any shape, `micTicNaive` for a grid mutual-information scan.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">ranksAverageTies</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span></code> | Ranks in 1..n, smallest value first, with tied values sharing the average of the positions they occupy: `3, 1, 4, 1, 5` comes back as `3.0, 1.5, 4.0, 1.5, 5.0`, since the two 1s sit at positions 1 and 2. The result therefore always sums to n(n+1)/2 whatever the input looks like. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">pearson</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Pearson's product-moment correlation, in -1..1: 1 is a perfect increasing straight line, -1 a perfect decreasing one, and 0 means no *linear* relationship — which is emphatically not the same as no relationship, as the symmetric parabola in `main` demonstrates. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">spearman</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Spearman's rank correlation — `pearson` applied to each array's `ranksAverageTies`, which puts a monotone-but-curved relationship at ±1 where Pearson reads less: exactly +1 for any strictly increasing pair, exactly -1 for any strictly decreasing one, whatever curve connects them. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">kendallTauB</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Kendall's tau-b, in -1..1: concordant minus discordant pairs over all pairs, corrected for ties in either variable. Like `spearman` it measures monotone rather than linear association, and the two agree in sign throughout; tau-b is the more conservative of the pair in magnitude. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">chatterjeeXi</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Chatterjee's xi, which is **asymmetric on purpose**: it measures how nearly `y` is a *function* of `x`, so swapping the arguments asks a different question and returns a different number. Near 0 for independence, near 1 when y is a noiseless function of x — including a non-monotone one such as a parabola, where `pearson` reads 0 and `kendallTauB` not much more. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">xi</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Short alias for `chatterjeeXi`, for when the formula rather than the surname is what you have in mind. Same asymmetry: the first argument is the predictor. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">distanceCorrelation</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Székely–Rizzo distance correlation, in 0..1 — and unlike `pearson` it is 0 *only* for genuine independence, which is what makes it the one to reach for when you do not want to guess the shape of the relationship first. It is symmetric in its arguments and never negative, so it tells you how much dependence there is and nothing at all about direction. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">MineLikeResult</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">mic</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">tic</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">bestXBins</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">bestYBins</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | What `micTicNaive` reports: the best (`mic`) and the summed (`tic`) normalized mutual-information score across every grid it scanned, plus the `bestXBins` × `bestYBins` grid that produced the maximum. Read the caveat on `micTicNaive` before trusting any of the four. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">micTicNaive</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">bMax</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MineLikeResult</span></code> | A MIC/TIC-style scan: bin x and y onto every grid whose cell count fits a budget, score normalized mutual information on each, and report the maximum and the sum. Unlike the correlation coefficients above it is blind to the *shape* of the relationship, so a parabola or a sine scores about as high as a straight line — which is the point of reaching for it. |

### RollingDistanceCorrelation { #correlations-kt-rollingdistancecorrelation }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">RollingDistanceCorrelation</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">windowSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

Distance correlation over a sliding window, maintained incrementally: `push` a sample pair, get the current 0..1 coefficient back, at O(w) work per sample for a window of w rather than the O(w²) rebuild `StatsDependence.distanceCorrelation` would charge you.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">push</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Push one (x,y) sample. If the window is full, evicts the oldest. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">current</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Current distance correlation (no mutation). |

### RollingXiCorrelation { #correlations-kt-rollingxicorrelation }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">RollingXiCorrelation</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">windowSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

Chatterjee's xi over a sliding window, recomputed from scratch on every push — no incremental trickery, just `StatsDependence.chatterjeeXi` over the window's current contents, which costs O(w log w) per sample and is exactly as trustworthy as the batch answer.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">push</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Push one (x, y) sample — evicting the oldest if the window is already full — and return xi over the window as it now stands, or null while fewer than two samples have arrived. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">current</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Xi over the window's current contents without pushing anything, or null while fewer than two samples have arrived. Copies the window out in arrival order first, which no longer matters to the answer: `StatsDependence.chatterjeeXi` sorts by x itself and resolves x-ties by expectation rather than by position, so the result depends only on *which* pairs are in the window and not on where in the ring buffer they happen to sit. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">clear</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Forget every buffered sample. The next `push` starts a fresh window and returns null again, exactly as it did on a new instance. |

## dirichlet.kt { #dirichlet-kt }

2D multiplicatively weighted Voronoi (Apollonius) diagrams. Each site is a `Vec3` of
`(x, y, weight)` and cells are decided by the score `|x - p|² / w²`.

`CircularDirichlet.build` returns a `Diagram` holding one `CellBoundary` per site, its pieces
sorted angularly around that site. Because the bisector of two differently weighted sites is a
circle — and a line only when the weights match — boundaries arrive as `ArcPiece` and
`LinePiece` rather than polygon edges; call `toPolyline` / `toPolylines` on a piece to
tessellate it, and pass an `Aabb` clip, since unbounded lines cannot be flattened without one
and clipping an arc may split it into several polylines.

All weights must be > 0 (`build` requires it). The construction is triple-nested over the
sites — every bisector is intersected against every other, and each candidate piece is kept
only if a midpoint sample really is on the cell boundary — so it is aimed at modest site
counts. Pure Kotlin on Field's `Vec2`/`Vec3`; the 3D counterpart is `CircularDirichlet3d` in
`voronoi.kt`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/dirichlet.kt`

## interpolants.kt { #interpolants-kt }

`smoothTo` wraps a target-producing lambda so that reading it eases toward the target instead
of jumping to it.

The returned `() -> T` is privately also a `HasUniform`/`ProgressingUniform`, so it can sit
where Field expects a uniform and be re-evaluated per frame. It implements
[`NeedsStartingValue`](math.md#interpolants-kt-needsstartingvalue), and whoever binds it is responsible for calling `startAt` with the
current value — until that happens the interpolant simply reports the target and marks itself
complete.

Interpolation is linear and only covers `Float`, `Double`, `Int`, `Long` and
`Vector2f`/`Vector3f`/`Vector4f`; any other type completes immediately at the target. Progress
is either time-based (`time` seconds), a fixed number of evaluations (`steps`, default 100), or
frame-based by supplying `clock = frameClock(fps) { frameNumber }`. Time-based interpolation uses
`System.nanoTime` by default; an injected clock makes offline and fixed-rate rendering independent
of scheduler pauses. The interpolation is one-shot: once it reaches the target it stays there.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/interpolants.kt`

**Used in:** [Values over time: interpolants & keyframes](../interpolants_examples.md)

## linalg.kt { #linalg-kt }

The short vector aliases ([`Vec2`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec2), `Vec3`, [`Vec4`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec4), [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat), [`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat)) plus the constructors and
point-cloud helpers that sit on top of Field's generated `afield.stdlib.linalg` types.

`vec(...)` is the usual way to make one — from numbers, by copying, or by concatenating a
scalar with a smaller vector — and `quat` / `dualquat` do the same for rotations. Collections
of vectors gain `center`, `median` / `medianVec` and `aabbBounds` in 2D, 3D and 4D; 3D also
gets `obbBounds` (PCA by power iteration, an explicit approximation — the code says so),
`convexHull`, which goes through the QuickHull3D library and returns the input unchanged if the
hull cannot be built, and `convexHullPeelingMedian`, which peels hulls away and returns the
centre of what is left — a single point, not a cloud. [`Cuboid`](math.md#linalg-kt-cuboid) is a separate plain 3D
box-with-size type used for layout-style union / inset / intersects work.

These vector types are mutable and most operations mutate the receiver, so copy first
(`Vec3(existing)`) when you need to keep the original. Swizzles and the *vector* `invoke`, `%=`
and `len` operators are deliberately absent here: they are generated for every float vector into
`Swizzles.kt` and `VectorOperators.kt` by `tools/linalg-generator`. `%=` for [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat) and
[`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat) is defined here, because no generator emits those.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/linalg.kt`

**Used in:** [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md), [Kotlin Syntax Overview (for Python + JavaScript folks)](../kotlin_overview.md), [Linear algebra in Field](../linear_algebra.md)

Infinities are not covered. |

Neither operand is modified. |

Size is unchanged. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">intersects</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">r</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Cuboid</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Do the two boxes overlap in volume? **Open** here, unlike the point overload: boxes that merely touch — one's face flush against the other's — do *not* intersect, which is what you want when packing things edge to edge. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | `Cuboid{x=… y=… z=… w=… h=… d=…}` — the corner and the size, for debugging. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">inset</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">by</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Cuboid</span></code> | A copy shrunk by `by` on **every** side: the corner moves in by that much and each dimension loses twice it. Negative values grow the box instead. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">intersectsX</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Does the box's x span cover the coordinate `x`? Half-open — `[this.x, this.x + w)` — so neighbouring spans laid end to end claim each coordinate exactly once. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">inside</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">start</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">end</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Is the box's x span **entirely within** `start..end`? Containment, not overlap; y and z are ignored. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">convert</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">z</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector3d</span></code> | Turns a normalized position in the box into a world one: `(0,0,0)` is the corner and `(1,1,1)` the far corner. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">duplicate</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Cuboid</span></code> | An identical copy. `Cuboid` is immutable, so this is only needed for identity, not for safety. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">equals</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Value equality on all six fields — exact `Float` comparison, so arithmetic drift will fail it. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">hashCode</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Consistent with `equals`: all six fields, so a `Cuboid` is safe as a map key. |

## math.kt { #math-kt }

`Number`-taking overloads of the trigonometric functions, so `sin(1)` and `sin(1f)` work
without writing `.toDouble()` at every call site.

Covers the circular functions and their inverses (`sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`,
`atan2`) and the hyperbolic ones (`sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `asinh`, `acosh`, `atanh`). Each is a
one-line delegate to the matching `kotlin.math` function and always returns `Double`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/math.kt`

### Top-level functions { #math-kt-functions }

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">sin</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Sine of `n` **radians**, in `-1..1`. Multiply by `PI / 180` first if you are thinking in degrees. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">cos</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Cosine of `n` **radians**, in `-1..1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">tan</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Tangent of `n` **radians**; unbounded, and enormous near odd multiples of `PI/2`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">asin</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Arc sine of `n`, in radians over `-PI/2..PI/2`. `NaN` outside the domain `-1..1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">acos</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Arc cosine of `n`, in radians over `0..PI`. `NaN` outside the domain `-1..1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">atan</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Arc tangent of `n`, in radians over `-PI/2..PI/2`. For a full-circle angle use `atan2`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">atan2</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The angle of the vector `(x, y)` in radians over `-PI..PI`, measured counter-clockwise from the positive x axis. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">sinh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Hyperbolic sine of `n`. Unbounded, and overflows to infinity somewhere past `n = 710`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">cosh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Hyperbolic cosine of `n`; `1` at zero and rising either side of it. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">tanh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Hyperbolic tangent of `n`, in `-1..1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">asinh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Inverse hyperbolic sine of `n`. Defined for every real input. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">acosh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Inverse hyperbolic cosine of `n`, `>= 0`. `NaN` below `n = 1`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">atanh</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Inverse hyperbolic tangent of `n`. Infinite at `±1` and `NaN` outside it — the inverse of `tanh`. |

## pf.kt { #pf-kt }

An unscented Kalman filter, and a particle filter whose particles each carry one.

[`UnscentedKalmanFilter`](math.md#pf-kt-unscentedkalmanfilter) keeps a mean and covariance and takes the transition and observation
models as lambdas; `UnscentedKalmanFilter.updateWithLikelihood` returns the log measurement
likelihood, which is exactly what [`UKFParticleFilter`](math.md#pf-kt-ukfparticlefilter) accumulates into each particle's log
weight. A [`UKFParticle`](math.md#pf-kt-ukfparticle) holds a UKF for the continuous state plus a hypothesis of your own
type `H` for the discrete or non-Gaussian part. `UKFParticleFilter.resampleIfNeeded` does
systematic resampling once the effective sample size drops below a fraction of the particle
count, and can immediately roughen the resampled means ([`RougheningOptions`](math.md#pf-kt-rougheningoptions)) so exact clones
separate again.

State and measurement dimensions are restricted to 1..3 — the private determinant helper only
covers those sizes and everything `require`s it. The linear algebra (`Matrix` is just
`Array<DoubleArray>`; Cholesky with escalating jitter, Gauss–Jordan inverse) is private to this
file, has no external dependency, and allocates fresh arrays on every step.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/pf.kt`

**Used in:** [State estimation: tracking what you cannot measure](../state_estimation_examples.md)

This is useful immediately after resampling, when many particles may be exact clones. |

## randoms.kt { #randoms-kt }

Box-scoped randomness. `random`, `randomGaussian` and `setRandomSeed` draw from a
`java.util.Random` held as a property on the current `Box`, so re-running a box replays the
same sequence; with no `Box` in context they fall back to one process-wide generator seeded
with `STDLIB_RANDOM_DEFAULT_SEED`.

Alongside the seed each box carries a noise phase you advance yourself (`noisePhase`,
`noiseForward`, `setNoisePhase`). That phase and seed drive `noise1D`, a small Perlin-style
hashed 1D noise, and the `perlinNoise` extensions on `Vector2f`/`Vector3f`/`Vector4f`, which
take one independent noise channel per component.

All the vector extensions — `perlinNoise` and the uniform-jitter `noise(d)` — mutate the
receiver in place and return it rather than allocating. `nextGaussian` is a Box-Muller
extension that fills the gap left by `kotlin.random.Random`, which has no Gaussian of its own.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/randoms.kt`

**Used in:** [State estimation: tracking what you cannot measure](../state_estimation_examples.md)

The Kotlin stdlib `Random` has no `nextGaussian()` of its own (unlike `java.util.Random`), so this fills the gap for code that carries its own seeded generator. |

Use to drive noise from a clock. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">noise1D</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">phase</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">currentStdlibPhase</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">seedOffset</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">frequency</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1f</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">extraHash</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Repeatable 1D Perlin-style noise: smooth, continuous, and bounded by **±0.5**. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Vector2f</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">perlinNoise</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">amplitude</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">phaseAdvance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0f</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">frequency</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1f</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">seedOffset</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">extraHash</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector2f</span></code> | Adds smooth `noise1D` wander to this point **in place**, one independent channel per component, and returns the same instance. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Vector3f</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">perlinNoise</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">amplitude</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">phaseAdvance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0f</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">frequency</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1f</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">seedOffset</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">extraHash</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector3f</span></code> | Adds smooth `noise1D` wander to this point **in place** — three independent channels, one per component — and returns the same instance. Conventions exactly as the `Vector2f` overload; this one consumes noise channels `seedOffset` through `seedOffset + 2`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Vector4f</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">perlinNoise</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">amplitude</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">phaseAdvance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0f</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">frequency</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1f</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">seedOffset</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">extraHash</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector4f</span></code> | Adds smooth `noise1D` wander to all four components **in place**, one independent channel each, and returns the same instance. Conventions as the `Vector2f` overload. Note that on a colour this wanders alpha too, which is rarely what you want — jitter the `Vector3f` and rebuild the alpha. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Vector2f</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">noise</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">d</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector2f</span></code> | Jitters this point **in place** by an independent uniform draw per component and returns the same instance. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Vector3f</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">noise</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">d</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector3f</span></code> | Jitters all three components **in place** by up to `±d/2` each, uniformly and independently, and returns the same instance. As the `Vector2f` overload: white noise, not smooth wander. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Vector4f</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">noise</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">d</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Number</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector4f</span></code> | Jitters all four components **in place** by up to `±d/2` each, uniformly and independently, and returns the same instance. As the `Vector2f` overload — including alpha, if this is a colour. |

## smile_interpolation_regression.kt { #smile-interpolation-regression-kt }

Two 1D fitters that wrap the Smile library: `smileCubicSpline` (cubic spline interpolation
through the data) and `smileGaussianProcess` (Gaussian-process regression with a Gaussian
kernel, configured by [`SmileGpOptions`](math.md#smile-interpolation-regression-kt-smilegpoptions)).

Both take parallel `xs`/`ys` arrays, copy them, and require at least two finite samples with
`xs` strictly increasing — a violation throws rather than producing a quietly bad fit. The
returned [`SmileCubicSpline1D`](math.md#smile-interpolation-regression-kt-smilecubicspline1d) / [`SmileGaussianProcess1D`](math.md#smile-interpolation-regression-kt-smilegaussianprocess1d) are callable via `invoke` and also
expose `predict` for a single `x` or for a whole array.

One caveat worth knowing: if Smile throws while fitting the GP, `smileGaussianProcess` prints
a warning to stderr and substitutes plain linear interpolation between the training points, so
holding a [`SmileGaussianProcess1D`](math.md#smile-interpolation-regression-kt-smilegaussianprocess1d) is not proof that a GP was actually fitted.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/smile_interpolation_regression.kt`
